Two glass plates are held a constant distance apart, forming a growing sheet of laminated glass resin. As rollers pull the plates apart, the length is increasing by $2\,\text{cm}\text{/min},$ while the $1\,\text{cm}$ thickness does not change. If resin is injected so that the volume of the sheet is increasing at a rate of $32\,{\text{cm}}^{3}\text{/min},$  how fast is its width changing when its dimensions are $10\,\text{cm}$ in length and $4\,\text{cm}$ in width?

The width is increasing at a rate of
{{field-1}}
$\text{cm}/\text{min}.$
questions.worked_solution:
Let $x,y,z$ be the dimensions of the solid, and let $V$ be its volume. We are given that 

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =10\,\text{cm}, \\ y & =4\,\text{cm}, \\ z & =1\,\text{cm}.\end{aligned}
$$

Also, we know that

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =2\,\text{cm}\text{/min}, \\ \frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =32\,{\text{cm}}^{3}\text{/min}.\end{aligned}
$$

We would like to find $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}$ when $x=10\,\text{cm},$ $y=4\,\text{cm}$ and $z=1\,\text{cm}.$

We start with the formula for the volume of the rectangular prism:

$$
V=xyz
$$

Since $z$ is not changing and $z=1,$ we get

$$
V=xy.
$$

Now, we differentiate with respect to time using the chain rule, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(xy) \\ \frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =x(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})+y(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}).\end{aligned}
$$

We can now plug in the known values into the above expression. This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}32 & =10(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})+4(2) \\ 32 & =10(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})+8 \\ 24 & =10(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}) \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =2.4\,\text{cm}\text{/min}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the width of the solid is increasing at a rate of $2.4\,\text{cm}/\text{min}$ at the moment when $x=10\,\text{cm},$ $y=4\,\text{cm}$ and $z=1\,\text{cm}.$

A sugar cube is dissolving uniformly in water. If the volume of the cube decreases at a rate of $48\,{\text{cm}}^{3}/\text{s},$ determine the rate at which the edges of the cube are decreasing when the volume of the cube is $8\,{\text{cm}}^{3}.$ Assume that the edge's rate of decrease is positive.

The edges of the cube are decreasing at a rate of
{{field-1}}
$\text{cm}/\text{s}.$
questions.worked_solution:
Let $x$ be the side of the cube and let $V$ be its volume. We are given that 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t}=-48\,{\text{cm}}^{3}/\text{s}.\end{aligned}
$$

We would like to find $\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}$ when $V=8\,{\text{cm}}^{3}.$

We start with the formula for the volume of the cube:

$$
V={x}^{3}
$$

Now, we differentiate with respect to time using the chain rule, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(V) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({x}^{3}) \\ \frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =3{x}^{2}\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Before we plug in the known values, we need to find the value of $x$ when $V=8\,{\text{cm}}^{3}.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}V & ={x}^{3} \\ 8 & ={x}^{3} \\ x & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now plug $x=2$ and $\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t}=-48$ into the expression for $\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}.$ This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =3{x}^{2}\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} \\ -48 & =3(2)^{2}\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} \\ -48 & =12\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} \\ \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =-4.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the edges of the cube are decreasing at a rate of $4\,\text{cm}/\text{s}$ at the moment when $x=2\,\text{cm}.$

The length of a rectangular prism is decreasing by $0.5\text{ feet}\text{/min}$ and its height increasing at a rate of $1\text{ feet/min}.$ If the volume of the rectangular prism is decreasing at a rate of $10{\text{ feet}}^{3}\text{/min},$  how fast is its width changing when its dimensions are $2\text{ feet}$ in length, $3\text{ feet}$ in width and $1\text{ feet}$ in height?
questions.worked_solution:
Let $x,y,z$ be the dimensions of the solid, and let $V$ be its volume. We are given that 

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =2\text{ feet}, \\ y & =1\text{ feet}, \\ z & =3\text{ feet}.\end{aligned}
$$

Also, we know that

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =-0.5\text{ feet}\text{/min}, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =1\text{ feet}\text{/min}, \\ \frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =-10{\text{ feet}}^{3}\text{/min}.\end{aligned}
$$

We would like to find $\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t}$ when $x=2\,\text{feet},$ $y=1\,\text{feet},$ and $z=3\,\text{feet}.$

We start with the formula for the volume of the rectangular prism:

$$
V=xyz
$$

Now, we differentiate with respect to time using the chain rule, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(x\cdot y\cdot z) \\ \frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =xy(\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t})+xz(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})+yz(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})\end{aligned}
$$

We can now plug in the known values into the above expression. This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}-10 & =(2)(1)(\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t})+(2)(3)(1)+(1)(3)(-0.5) \\ \frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t} & =-7.25\text{ feet}\text{/min}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the width of the solid is decreasing at a rate of $7.25\,\text{feet}/\text{min}$ at the moment when $x=2\,\text{feet},$ $y=1\,\text{feet},$ and $z=3\,\text{feet}.$

A cube is expanding uniformly at a rate of $135{\text{ cm}}^{3}\text{/s}.$ How fast is each edge of the cube increasing when the volume of the cube is $125{\text{ cm}}^{3}?$
questions.worked_solution:
Let $x$ be the side length of the cube and let $V$ be its volume. We are given that 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t}=135\,{\text{cm}}^{3}/\text{s}.\end{aligned}
$$

We would like to find $\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}$ when $V=125\,{\text{cm}}^{3}.$

We start with the formula for the volume of the cube:

$$
V={x}^{3}
$$

Now, we differentiate with respect to time using the chain rule, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(V) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({x}^{3}) \\ \frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =3{x}^{2}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Before we plug in the known values, we need to find the value of $x$ when $V=125\,{\text{cm}}^{3}.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}V & ={x}^{3} \\ 125 & ={x}^{3} \\ x & =5.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now plug $x=5$ and $\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t}=135$ into the expression for $\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}.$ This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =3{x}^{2}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} \\ 135 & =3(5)^{2}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\, \\ \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{9}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the sides of the cube are increasing at a rate of $\frac{9}{5}\,\text{cm}/\text{s}$ at the moment when $x=5\,\text{cm}.$

The length of the rectangular prism shown above is increasing, while the $4\,\text{in}$ width and the $6\,\text{in}$ height don't change. What is the rate of change of the length of the rectangular prism if the volume is increasing at a rate of $72\,{\text{in}}^{3}/\text{min}?$
questions.worked_solution:
Let $x,y,z$ be the dimensions of the rectangular prism, let $V$ be its volume. We are given that 

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =4\,\text{in}, \\ z & =6\,\text{in}.\end{aligned}
$$

Also, we know that

$$
\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t}=72\,{\text{in}}^{3}/\text{min}.
$$

We would like to find $\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}$ when $y=4\,\text{in}$ and $z=6\,\text{in}.$

We start with the formula for the volume of the rectangular prism:

$$
V=xyz
$$

Substituting the known values, we get

$$
V=x(4)(6)=24x.
$$

Now, we differentiate with respect to time using the chain rule, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(24x) \\ \frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =24(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}).\end{aligned}
$$

We can now plug in the known value into the above expression. This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}72 & =24(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}) \\ \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =3\,\text{in}\text{/min}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the length of the rectangular prism is increasing at a rate of $3\,\text{in}/\text{min}.$

An elastic rectangular prism whose height is $15\text{ in}$ and width is $24\text{ in}$ is being stretched. If its length is increasing at a rate of $8\text{ in/min},$ what is the rate of change of the surface area of the rectangular prism?

The surface area is increasing at a rate of
{{field-1}}
${\text{in}}^{2}/\text{min}.$
questions.worked_solution:
Let $x,y,z$ be the dimensions of the rectangular prism, let $S$ be its surface area, and let $V$ be its volume. The variables $x,S,$ and $V$ change with time. In particular, we are given that 

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =15\text{ in}, \\ z & =24\text{ in}, \\ \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =8\text{ in}\text{/min}.\end{aligned}
$$

We would like to find $\frac{\text{d}S}{\text{d}t}.$

We want to find the rate of change of $S$ knowing the rate of change of $x.$ So, we start with the formula for the surface area of the rectangular prism:

$$
S=2xz+2xy+2yz
$$

Substituting the known values, we get

$$
S=2(x)(24)+2x(15)+2(15)(24)=78x+720.
$$

Now, we differentiate with respect to time using the chain rule, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}S}{\text{d}t} & =78(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}).\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the above expression using $\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}=8,$ and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}S}{\text{d}t} & =78(8)=624.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the rectangular prism's surface area is increasing at a rate of $624\,{\text{in}}^{2}/\text{min}.$

In a laboratory, a researcher is increasing the edges of an iron cube at a rate of $0.5\text{ feet/min}.$ How fast is the surface area changing when each edge is $3\text{ feet?}$
questions.worked_solution:
Let $x$ be the side of the cube, let $S$ be its surface area, and let $V$ be its volume. All of the variables change with time. In particular, we are given that 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}=0.5\,\text{feet}/\text{min}.\end{aligned}
$$

We would like to find $\frac{\text{d}S}{\text{d}t}$ when $x=3\,\text{feet}.$

We want to find the rate of change of $S$ knowing the rate of change of $x.$ So, we start with the formula for the surface area of the cube:

$$
S=6{x}^{2}
$$

Now, we differentiate with respect to time using the chain rule, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(S) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(6{x}^{2}) \\ \frac{\text{d}S}{\text{d}t} & =12x\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now plug in the known values into the above expression. This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}S}{\text{d}t} & =12x\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} \\ \frac{\text{d}S}{\text{d}t} & =12(3)(0.5) \\ \frac{\text{d}S}{\text{d}t} & =18.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the cube's surface area is changing at a rate of $18\,{\text{feet}}^{2}/\text{min}.$

A worker is coating a surface with epoxy using a thickness gauge, which fixes the epoxy height at $5\,\text{in}.$ If the length is increasing at a rate of $3\,\text{in}\text{/s}$ and the width is increasing at a rate of $2\,\text{in}\text{/s},$ how fast is the surface area of the epoxy layer increasing when its length is $12\,\text{in}$ and its width is $7\,\text{in}?$

The surface area is increasing at a rate of
{{field-1}}
${\text{in}}^{2}/\text{s}.$
questions.worked_solution:
Let $x,y,z$ be the dimensions of the solid, and let $S$ be its surface area. We are given that 

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =12\,\text{in}, \\ y & =7\,\text{in}, \\ z & =5\,\text{in}, \\ \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =3\,\text{in}\text{/s}, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =2\,\text{in}\text{/s}.\end{aligned}
$$

We would like to find $\frac{\text{d}S}{\text{d}t}.$

We want to find the rate of change of $S$ knowing the rate of change of $x$ and $y.$ So, we start with the formula for the surface area of the rectangular prism:

$$
S=2xz+2xy+2yz
$$

Since $z=5\,\text{in}$ is not changing, we get

$$
S=10x+2xy+10y.
$$

Now, we differentiate with respect to time using the chain rule, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}S}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(10x+2xy+10y) \\ \frac{\text{d}S}{\text{d}t} & =(10+2x)(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})+(10+2y)(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}).\end{aligned}
$$

We can now plug in the known values into the above expression. This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}S}{\text{d}t} & =(10+2\cdot 12)(2)+(10+2\cdot 7)(3) \\  & =(34)(2)+(24)(3) \\  & =68+72 \\  & =140\,{\text{in}}^{2}\text{/s}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the surface area of the rectangular prism is increasing at a rate of $140\,{\text{in}}^{2}/\text{s}.$

The length of a rectangular prism is decreasing at a rate of $4\,\text{cm}\text{/min},$ the width is increasing at a rate of $5\,\text{cm}\text{/min},$ and the $6\,\text{cm}$ height does not change. How fast is the surface area of the rectangular prism decreasing when its dimensions are $4\,\text{cm}$ in length and $11\,\text{cm}$ in width?
questions.worked_solution:
Let $x,y,z$ be the dimensions of the solid, and let $S$ be its surface area. We are given that 

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =4\,\text{cm}, \\ y & =11\,\text{cm}, \\ z & =6\,\text{cm}, \\ \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =-4\,\text{cm}\text{/min}, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =5\,\text{cm}\text{/min}.\end{aligned}
$$

We would like to find $\frac{\text{d}S}{\text{d}t}.$

We want to find the rate of change of $S$ knowing the rate of change of $x$ and $y.$ So, we start with the formula for the surface area of the rectangular prism:

$$
S=2xz+2xy+2yz
$$

Since $z=6\,\text{cm}$ is not changing, we get

$$
S=12x+2xy+12y.
$$

Now, we differentiate with respect to time using the chain rule, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}S}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(12x+2xy+12y) \\ \frac{\text{d}S}{\text{d}t} & =(2x+12)(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})+(12+2y)(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}).\end{aligned}
$$

We can now plug in the known values into the above expression. This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}S}{\text{d}t} & =(2\cdot 4+12)(5)+(12+2\cdot 11)(-4) \\  & =100-136 \\  & =-36\,{\text{cm}}^{2}\text{/min}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the surface area of the rectangular prism is decreasing at a rate of $36\,{\text{cm}}^{2}/\text{min}.$

A rectangular block of ice is melting in a narrow channel that keeps its length fixed at $12\,\text{in}.$ Its width is decreasing by $1\,\text{in}\text{/h},$ while its height is decreasing by $0.4\,\text{in}\text{/h}.$ How fast is its volume decreasing when its dimensions are $5\,\text{in}$ in width and $4\,\text{in}$ in height? Assume that the volume's rate of decrease is positive.

The volume is decreasing at a rate of
{{field-1}}
${\text{in}}^{3}/\text{h}.$
questions.worked_solution:
We define the following variables:

- let $L,$ $W,$ and $H$ be the length, width, and height of the ice block, respectively, and

- let $V$ be the volume of the ice block.

Note that $H,$ $W,$ and $V$ change with time, while $L$ is constant. 

We are given that

$$
\begin{aligned}L=12\text{ in},\, & W=5\text{ in}, \\ H=4\text{ in},\, & \frac{\text{d}W}{\text{d}t}=-1\text{ in/h}, \\ \frac{\text{d}H}{\text{d}t}=-0.4\text{ in/h}\end{aligned}
$$

We would like to find $\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t}.$

The relation between the three time-dependent variables, $V,$ $W$ and $H,$ is given by the formula for the volume of ice block:

$$
V=LWH
$$

We differentiate both sides of $V=LWH$ with respect to $t,$ treating $L$ as a constant, and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}V & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(LWH) \\ \frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =L\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(WH) \\ \frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =L[W(\frac{\text{d}H}{\text{d}t})+H(\frac{\text{d}W}{\text{d}t})] \\ \frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =L\cdot W(\frac{\text{d}H}{\text{d}t})+L\cdot H(\frac{\text{d}W}{\text{d}t}).\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can plug in the known values and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =(12)(5)(-0.4)+(12)(4)(-1) \\ \frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =-24+(-48) \\ \frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =-72.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the volume of ice is decreasing at a rate of $72\,{\text{in}}^{3}\text{/h}.$

A rectangular swimming pool (with a horizontal bottom) is being drained. If its length and width are $25\text{ m}$ and $15\text{ m}$, respectively, and the water level is falling at a rate of $0.25\,\text{m/min},$ how fast is the water draining out of the pool?
questions.worked_solution:
We define the following variables:

- let $L$ and $W$ be the length and width of the swimming pool, respectively, and

- let $h$ and $V$ be the height and volume of the water, respectively.

Note that $h$ and $V$ change with time, while $L$ and $W$ are constants. 

We are given that

$$
L=25\,\text{m},\,W=15\,\text{m},\,\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t}=-0.25\,\text{m}/\text{min}.
$$

We would like to find $\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t}.$

The relation between the two time-dependent variables, $V$ and $h,$ is given by the formula for the volume of water:

$$
V=LWh
$$

We differentiate both sides of $V=LWh$ with respect to $t,$ treating both $L$ and $W$ as constants, and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}V & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(LWh) \\ \frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =LW\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can plug in the known values and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =(25)(15)\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t} \\ \frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =375\cdot (-0.25) \\ \frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =-93.75.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the water is draining out at a rate of $93.75\,{\text{m}}^{3}\text{/min}.$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}V & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(LWH) \\ \frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =W\cdot H(\frac{\text{d}L}{\text{d}t})+L\cdot H(\frac{\text{d}W}{\text{d}t})+L\cdot W(\frac{\text{d}H}{\text{d}t}).\end{aligned}

The edges of a cube decrease at a rate of $9\text{ cm/s}.$ At what rate is the volume decreasing when the length of each edge is $40\text{ cm}?$
questions.worked_solution:
Let $x$ be the side length of the cube and let $V$ be its volume. We are given that 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}=-9\text{ cm/s}.\end{aligned}
$$

We would like to find $\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t}$ when $x=40\text{ cm}.$

We start with the formula for the volume of the cube:

$$
V={x}^{3}
$$

Now, we differentiate with respect to time using the chain rule, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(V) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({x}^{3}) \\ \frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =3{x}^{2}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now plug $x=40$ and $\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}=-9\text{ cm/s}$ into the expression for $\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t}.$ This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =3{x}^{2}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} \\ \frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =3(40)^{2}\cdot (-9)\, \\ \frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =-43\,200.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the volume of the cube is decreasing at a rate of $43\,200{\text{ cm}}^{3}\text{/s}$ at the moment when $x=40\,\text{cm}.$

canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Let $x$ be the side of the cube and $V$ be its volume. We are given that 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t}=-3\,{\text{mm}}^{3}/\text{s}.\end{aligned}
$$

We would like to find $\dfrac{\textrm d x}{\textrm dt}$ when $V=27\,\text{mm}^3.$

We start with the formula for the volume of the cube:

$$
V=x^3
$$

Now, we differentiate with respect to time using the chain rule, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}V & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({x}^{3}) \\ \frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =3{x}^{2}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Before we plug in the known values, we need to find the value of $x$ when $V = 27\,\text{mm}^3.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}V & ={x}^{3} \\ 27 & ={x}^{3} \\ x & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now plug $x=3$ and $\dfrac{\textrm d V}{\textrm dt}=-3$ into the expression for $\dfrac{\textrm d x}{\textrm dt}.$ This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =3{x}^{2}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} \\ -3 & =3(3)^{2}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\, \\ \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =-\frac{1}{9}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the sides of the cube are shrinking at a rate of $\dfrac{1}{9}\,\text{mm}/\text{s}$ at the moment when $x=3\,\textrm{mm}.$

We differentiate both sides with respect to $t,$ treating both $L$ and $W$ as constants, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(V) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(LWh) \\ \frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =LW\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can plug in the known values and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =(20)(15)\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t} \\ \frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =300\cdot \frac{1}{6} \\ \frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =50.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the water level is rising at a rate of $50\,\text{ft}^3\textrm{/min}.$
